episodes.212072: An upper level disturbance moving across the central Rockies combined with higher moisture across the southeast plains of NM resulted in the development of multiple severe thunderstorms across southern Roosevelt County during the mid afternoon to mid evening hours. These thunderstorms resulted in three rounds of hail up to ping pong diameter between Pep and the Roosevelt and Lea County border. Back building of severe thunderstorms across this area resulted in some minor flooding in culverts and low lying areas. Thunderstorms tapered off just before sunset on May 21st due to the loss of daytime heating. Two more rounds of thunderstorms developed across the northeast and east central plains of NM during the afternoon on May 22nd and 23rd. These storms resulted in a severe wind gust at a public weather station near Melrose on May 22nd and at Tucumcari Municipal Airport on May 23rd. Storms exited into west Texas during the evening hours. The Trigg wildfire was also discovered in far eastern San Miguel County, burning through May 25th before coming under control.
episodes.212094: A series of mini-supercells developed during the late morning into the early afternoon hours. One of the thunderstorms produced a tornado in northeast Cullman County.  Repetitive rainfall caused excessive rainfall and flash flooding across parts of Cullman County.
episodes.212261: Pulses in the southwesterly flow aloft, coupled with the remnants of the stalled boundary from the 19th and 20th, allowed for more thunderstorms to develop on the 21st. One storm managed to produce quarter-sized hail in Lea county. High based showers in far west Texas also produced a couple of severe downbursts.
episodes.212262: Pulses in the southwesterly flow aloft, coupled with the remnants of the stalled boundary from the 19th and 20th, allowed for more thunderstorms to develop on the 21st. One storm managed to produce quarter-sized hail in Lea county. High based showers in far west Texas also produced a couple of severe downbursts.
episodes.212483: Numerous showers and thunderstorms occurred across Central Alabama during the late morning to early afternoon of May 22. Enough shear and instability were present to promote the development of small, low-topped supercells within a tropical environment. A few of these cells produced brief rotation, and three brief tornadoes occurred in Marengo and Tuscaloosa counties.
episodes.212497: A weak short wave trough moved overhead on the evening of the 21st within the larger cyclonic flow aloft. Most of region remained cool and stable with cloud cover persisting for much of the day. Areas across New Mexico saw clearing in the afternoon which allowed isolated thunderstorms to develop and drift into West Texas. One of these storms moved into western Cochran County producing penny size hail near Bledsoe.
episodes.212653: Scattered thunderstorms developed ahead of a dryline and cold front on the afternoon of the 22nd. Storms were initially transient and struggled to become organized due to a lack of deep layer shear across the region. However, numerous outflow boundary formed which initiated new convection and were able to take advantage of a moist and unstable atmosphere. Hail as large as tennis balls were observed in Hale County. The numerous outflow boundaries created enough shear to generate several landspout tornadoes across the area. None of the many landspout tornadoes caused any known damage. Additionally, merging storms in southeastern Hale County produced torrential rainfall which led to flash flooding of roads and fields north of Petersburg.
episodes.213028: A diffuse frontal boundary stalled across the northern forecast area 5/22 with broad troughing present. Areas south of the boundary saw generous heating with MLCAPE values nearing 1500-2000 J/kg and weak deep layer shear near 25-30 kts. This heating across the boundary lead to a couple strong storms, but one that produced tree damage near Thomson GA.
episodes.213468: A deepening High Plains low pressure, in concert with rapidly returning moisture ahead of a strong upper level disturbance approaching from the west, supported isolated to widely scattered strong to severe thunderstorms moving east to southeast over portions of east-central and northeast Colorado during the evening hours on the 21st. Hail reached tennis ball size in Kit Carson County.
episodes.213469: Outflow from showers moving east over the southern half of Wichita County caused a 63 mph wind gust just south of Leoti.
episodes.213565: An area of showers and thunderstorms developed over portions of northeastern Oklahoma during the early morning hours of the 22nd. This activity produced moderate to heavy rainfall that was persistent across the same area for several hours, resulting in rainfall amounts of three to seven inches. Flash flooding occurred in Tulsa and Rogers Counties from this heavy rainfall.
episodes.213570: Clusters of showers and thunderstorms affected the area for multiple days ahead of a cold front. Some storms were severe with impacts to trees and power lines.
episodes.213616: Scattered thunderstorms occurred ahead of a frontal boundary on May 22-25. However, on May 25, a mesoscale convective system developed west of the area and enhanced the low level wind field.  This resulted in two tornadoes across the tri-state area. One tornado affected the Villa Tasso area in Walton county in Florida, and the other tornado affected Houston and Henry counties in Alabama.  Both tornadoes were rated EF1.
episodes.213658: A tornadic supercell thunderstorm that was unusually weak from a tornadic storm perspective produced a brief and weak tornado in New Tazewell. Surface warm front draped across the state provided 15 to 20 knots of 1 km shear, and a handful of weakly rotating supercells formed and moved across northeastern Tennessee. The middle cell of three produced a tornado. This was the first tornado of the year for East Tennessee.
episodes.213720: A few severe storms produced damaging winds which downed trees across portions of central and southern Mississippi. A brief, weak tornado also occurred near Midway Road in Hinds County.
episodes.213752: During the late afternoon of May 22, 2026, low-topped supercell thunderstorms developed along a cold front advancing across eastern Nebraska and northwest Iowa. At 4:42 PM CST, one of these discrete cells produced a brief tornado in Cass County, Nebraska. The tornado was visually confirmed and photographed by multiple trained spotters. No damage was reported.
episodes.213825: Broad southwesterly flow aloft on the eastern side of a western CONUS trough carried several weak disturbances across the central Gulf Coast, while southeasterly low-level flow maintained deep moisture. Scattered afternoon thunderstorms developed across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi. A thunderstorm over the local marine areas produced a waterspout near the Interstate 10 Twin Span as well as severe wind gusts at other coastal locations.
episodes.213827: An embedded shortwave moved northeast through a broad upper-level trough while increasing midlevel winds aided thunderstorm organization across the central Gulf Coast. Ample atmospheric moisture in the local soundings and strong instability supported expanding afternoon convection with very efficient rainfall. Stronger cells produced damaging winds and large hail from the northshore and southshore of Lake Pontchartrain.
episodes.213828: An embedded shortwave moved northeast through a broad upper-level trough while increasing midlevel winds aided thunderstorm organization across the central Gulf Coast. Ample atmospheric moisture in the local soundings and strong instability supported expanding afternoon convection with very efficient rainfall. Storms aligned with the southwesterly steering flow, allowing localized training and flash flooding near Gulfport.
episodes.213968: As the third week of May 2026 unfolded, the dynamic breakup front stalled repeatedly along the Lower Yukon, creating a cascading sequence of severe jams and flooding. This period involved massive downstream surges as well as backwater effects in tributaries like the Andreafsky and Chuilnuk.
episodes.214064: A few severe thunderstorms produced large hail across the Concho Valley and Northern Edwards Plateau. Also, a lightning strike destroyed a hotel in Brady.
episodes.214085: Scattered thunderstorms developed across the South Carolina Piedmont during the afternoon and early evening in association with a stalled front. Several of the storms produced brief damaging wind gusts.
episodes.214140: A unique event with limited severe weather and flash flooding occurred during the evening hours on May 22nd. A surface low pressure system slowly moved across western Kentucky, with a warm front extending to the east-northeast across much of Kentucky. Along and south of this warm front, precipitable water values exceeding 1.7 inches lead to showers and a few thunderstorms which produced efficient rainfall rates. Where heavier showers and storms trained over eastern Shelby, Henry, and western Franklin County, a few instances of flash flooding were observed. Closer to the surface low pressure center, marginal amounts of instability (around 250-500 J/kg MLCAPE) combined with relatively impressive amounts of low-level shear and helicity along the warm front to produce miniature supercells. One of these mini supercells produced a brief EF0 tornado in Butler County near Butler County High School.
episodes.214401: As a strong wave sheared northward through the Dakotas, the right entrance region of an upper level jet interacted with a slow moving surface boundary to increase late day backing of wind fields and convergence.  While overall thermodynamic parameters were lacking, favorable overlap of near-surface vorticity and acceleration of near-surface parcels resulted in low-level rotating storms.  One storm anchored near the boundary produced a brief tornado.
episodes.214431: A tornadic supercell developed near or along the Kenedy/Kleberg County line during the evening of May 20, 2026. The storm tracked southeastward through Kenedy County before weakening just offshore Kenedy County that evening. A large hail and a very high wind gust (possible tornado) was reported as the supercell moved southeast and crossed Laguna Madre toward the nearshore Gulf waters.

This weak tornado tracked north northeastward roughly along Midway Road from north of Oakley Palestine Road to Thigpen Road, then lifted near Seven Springs Road. Along the path, several large tree limbs were downed. A tornadic debris signature (TDS) was observed on radar. Maximum winds were estimated at 75 mph (EF-0), the track length was 1.98 miles, and the maximum width was 175 yards.

A tornado developed along Sparks Road, east of Demopolis, near the Marengo County/Hale County line, where several hardwood trees were snapped and uprooted, and a residence had siding damage either from wind or fallen trees. The tornado then moved northeast and impacted homes just off Highway 80 near Yellow Creek Road. Shingles and siding were removed from a couple of homes, a shed was destroyed, and general yard items were strewn. Perhaps the most eye-catching item was the displacement and flipping of a box truck and a pontoon boat. The tornado then crossed Highway 80 with minimal signs of damage and came to an end just past the Hale County line, along Mount Olive Road, where tree branches were broken. Maximum winds were estimated at 95 mph.

A brief tornado occurred in the Exmoor community along County Road 6, between County Road 7 and Lewis Road. The tornado began along the back tree line of a property then moved northeast where it shifted a camper northward a few feet off of its cinder block supports. A manufactured home suffered damage to its porch and awning. Some trees were snapped and uprooted as the tornado crossed County Road 6 before dissipating as it downed trees across the road. Maximum winds were estimated at 65 mph.

An EF1 tornado entered Hale County from Marengo County came to an end just past the Hale County line, along Mount Olive Road, where tree branches were broken. Damage in Hale County was of EF0 intensity.

The tornado touched down just north of Interstate 20/59 nearly 2 miles east of exit 89 in a largely open field with a few trees here and there, one of which was uprooted. Numerous video recordings on social media showed a lowering cloudbase and nebulous funnel cloud crossing the interstate, with what looked like a very narrow drill bit tornado finally touching down. From there, the tornado moved north, crossing Union Road, where minor damage occurred to a double wide manufactured home and the first hint of a debris signature appeared. The tornado then traversed inaccessible forests and fields and intensified before reaching K and R Road, where several hardwood and softwood trees were snapped or uprooted. Only minor damage occurred to any homes on the street. The tornado then turned more northeasterly, crossed Bama Rock Garden Road where a carport was tossed and a home sustained other minor damage and crossed Charles Brook Rd, snapping and uprooting several trees. The tornado dissipated over inaccessible forest somewhere beyond Charles Brook Rd. Maximum winds were estimated at 95 mph.

The tornado touched down just north of U.S. Highway 278 and west of Holly Pond near the intersection of County Roads 1650 and 1682. There, it quickly assumed EF1 status, uprooting a hardwood tree, and causing door damage to small farm outbuildings nearby.  The tornado tracked generally northeastward, uprooting and snapping large hardwood trees along County Road 1683. Farther northeast, near the intersection of County Roads 1709, 1710, and 1711, multiple hardwood trees were snapped and uprooted, and in a small neighborhood there, a house experienced roof damage.  The tornado continued to track generally northeastward across a mix of open farmland and woodland, with snapped and uprooted hardwood trees again observed along County Road 1716.  To the northeast in the Brooklyn community, the tornado uprooted and snapped hardwood trees along County Road 1684, and minor roof damage occurred to a single family dwelling. There were also two cattle deaths due to tree falls off of County Road 1684. The tornado crossed northward on the east side of Brooklyn, and headed farther northeast to the east side of Baileyton, where it occasionally snapped and uprooted hardwood trees along the way.  Just to the northeast of Baileyton along County Road 1762, the tornado caused tree damage, with one large tree falling on and damaging a truck. Roof damage also occurred to a nearby house.  Farther northeast along County Road 1763, the tornado uprooted hardwood and softwood trees, pushed a mobile home off its foundation, and caused significant roof damage to the dwelling.  The tornado began curving slightly westward as it neared the intersections of Highway 67 and 69, causing sporadic tree damage along the way and also along Apple Grove Road. The tornado then tracked north-northwestward, ending on County Road 1589 just west of Highway 67.
